chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Waddad al-Hannat from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a woman who claimed against her husband that he had divorced her with one divorce, a valid divorce of the waiting period, meaning during purity from non-consummation, and he had testified for her with witnesses on that. Then the husband denied it afterwards, so he said: 'If he denied the divorce before the expiry of the waiting period, then his denial of the divorce is a revocation (raj'ah) for her. And if he denied the divorce after the expiry of the waiting period, then it is upon the Imam to separate them after the testimony of the witnesses, after being sworn that his denial of the divorce was after the expiry of the waiting period.'

key_terms.اَلْإِمَامُ: The Imam (or judge) who executes the separation
key_terms.اَلْعِدَّةِ: The waiting period for a divorced woman
key_terms.رَجْعَةٌ: Revocation (the husband's right to take back his wife during iddah)
key_terms.طَلاَقَ اَلْعِدَّةِ: Divorce during the waiting period (one of the three types of talaq)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling when a husband denies a divorce after the waiting period has expired?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the procedural nuances of *talaq al-'iddah* (divorce during purity without intercourse), a specific category in Shia jurisprudence. It establishes that a husband's pre-iddah denial functions as an automatic revocation (*raj'ah*), while post-iddah denial requires judicial intervention (*faskh*) contingent upon the husband's oath, highlighting the Imam's role in validating the timeline of the divorce. This mechanism underscores the importance of temporal precision in marital dissolution within the Twelver school.
